public_rationale: In May 2024, James Zou described increasing difficulty recruiting qualified reviewers for AI and computer-science conferences (e2). Springer Nature's 2025 annual report describes its Snapp review platform and says investment is helping it manage growing submission volumes (e3). The conference account does not establish sustained breakdown across journals attributable to LLM-generated submissions, and the publisher disclosure does not independently establish screening effectiveness (e2, e3). These items settle neither broad incapacity nor successful adaptation (e2, e3).
limitations: The recruitment account concerns conferences in limited disciplines and does not isolate the effect of LLM-generated submissions (e2).
Springer Nature's disclosure covers one publisher, and the cited technology section is explicitly unaudited (e3).
The evidence lacks representative measurements jointly tracking LLM-generated submissions, review capacity, backlogs and screening effectiveness.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Reviewers and journals will not be able to keep up with the flood of LLM-generated submissions.

statement.excerpt: And there is no way reviewers and journals are going to be able to keep up.

from_speaker: going to be able to keep up
tripling their workload would not be feasible
our_interpretation: Keeping up means maintaining workable review capacity and effective screening as LLM-generated submissions increase.
The claim concerns a broad failure across scientific publishing, rather than the existence of individual missed errors.
Tripling is a hypothetical illustration, not an explicit antecedent or a committed forecast of submission volume.
criteria.support_condition: Dated evidence establishes sustained, widespread review or screening breakdown across journals caused materially by increased LLM-generated submissions.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative evidence shows journals maintaining review capacity and screening effectiveness despite the substantial LLM-generated submission burden contemplated by the claim.

evidence.locator: James Zou interview, answer about differences between disciplines
evidence.publisher: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
evidence.explanation: Zou describes recruitment pressure alongside growing AI and computer-science conference submissions. This firsthand account does not establish system-wide journal failure or isolate the effect of LLM-generated submissions.

evidence.locator: Annual Report 2025, printed page 20, technology and AI box
evidence.explanation: The publisher describes an operating review platform and tools intended to accommodate growing volumes. This is counterevidence to inevitable incapacity, but publisher self-reporting does not establish independent screening effectiveness.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Cross-publisher operational records and independent audits showing whether measured growth in LLM-generated submissions causes sustained review or screening breakdown, or whether capacity and screening remain effective under that burden. An agreed observation period would be needed for a final failure-to-occur judgment.
